beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jow-hway Lee's Dusk Duel is a 2D fighting game. Assignment six adds two particle effects: a hit spark where a punch lands, and faint embers drifting through the courtyard while the fight runs. Jow-hway wrote the brief, every setting and every prediction. Claude Code and its agents built the scenes, the controllers and the tests.

beats.narration_text: Here's the game, an engine capture with scripted input. On the title screen, no embers. Enter starts the round, and the moment the fight begins, a thin field of embers is already there. Every punch that lands throws a burst of cyan particles around the white star, which is the old code-drawn spark the game already had.

beats.narration_text: Effect A, the hit spark. Its job, in Jow-hway's brief: confirm that an attack connected, at the exact contact point. The event is attack resolved, with result hit, at the overlap of hitbox and hurtbox. The intent: a compact flash, sparks outward for a fifth of a second, faded by point six. Cool white against a dark band, still three to one beside the brightest lantern. Four pooled slots of twenty.

beats.narration_text: Claude's reading of that strip, which is a claim, not a verdict: at frames twelve to fifteen the sparks sit on one ring with an empty middle, because they all leave at nearly the same speed. Jow-hway picked: it reads as a ring, from Claude's options, so this revision depends on that reading. One change: minimum speed, forty-five down to fifteen. Claude predicted a filled cluster, with the same outer edge.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole effect as a scene file, and the three parts of any particle system. Emission: line nineteen, twenty particles; line twenty-two, one shot; line twenty-five, all at once, from a point. Process, how each particle moves: line twenty-eight spreads them all ways, line twenty-nine adds gravity, line thirty is the revised minimum speed. Draw: line twenty, the star texture, and line seventeen, the additive material.

line 30 highlights: process: min speed, revised

beats.narration_text: And this is what those lines draw, before and after. The ring is gone: frames twelve and fifteen are a filled cluster. But Claude's prediction about the edge was wrong. The burst shrank, from fifty-eight pixels across to forty-eight, because each spark's speed is drawn between the minimum and the maximum, so lowering the minimum slows nearly all of them. Still inside the brief. Jow-hway's verdict: yes, I saw the ring. Keep.

beats.narration_text: In the game, a pool script starts a spark on every hit. Line forty-three takes the first slot that isn't still emitting, so a second hit never restarts a live burst; if all four are busy, line forty-five takes the oldest. Line forty-seven puts it at the contact point. Line fifty-six freezes all four during pause and hitstop, because neither pauses the scene tree.

line 45 highlights: all four busy: the oldest
line 47 highlights: at the contact point
line 56 highlights: frozen in pause and hitstop

props.title: Four Slots, Never Restarted
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/effects/hit_spark_pool.gd lines 43-56 · source 840bcfd · agent, slot fix by Claude Code
props.code:
var i := busy.find(false)
	if i < 0:
		i = started.find(started.min())
	var slot := slots[i]
	slot.position = point
	slot.restart()
	busy[i] = true
	started[i] = _next
	_next += 1


## Rule 5: the game's pause and hitstop do not pause the tree, so the emitters are frozen here.
func _apply_speed() -> void:
	var s := 0.0 if (main.paused or main.hitstop > 0) else 1.0

beats.narration_text: Effect B, courtyard embers. Its job is ambience: air and warmth, never competing with the fighters. The condition: run only while the phase is fight. And it uses two things the hit spark doesn't: a rectangular emission area, five hundred sixty by one eighty pixels over the arena, and a pree-process of one and a half seconds, so the field already exists when it starts.

Jow-hway's first look came as three multiple-choice answers to Claude's questions: already filled, too faint, faded out slowly. Claude's count agreed: about two hundred changed pixels out of nine hundred thousand. And frame ten was already populated, so pree-process runs when emitting turns on.

beats.narration_text: Embers are started and stopped by a small controller that polls the phase every physics tick. Line twenty-eight: entering the fight calls restart, so pree-process runs again every round. Line thirty: leaving the fight stops emitting, and live embers finish their lifetime. Like the pool, it also sets speed scale to zero during pause and hitstop.

show.event: line 30 highlights: leave fight: stop emitting

props.title: Start And Stop
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/effects/embers_controller.gd lines 20-33 · source 840bcfd · agent, approved by Claude Code under Zhaohui's delegation
props.code:
func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var fight: bool = main.phase == "fight"
	if fight and not _in_fight:
		# Rule 1 says "emitting = true"; restart() also sets emitting to true, and resets the
		# emitter's time so preprocess (1.5 s) runs again in every round, as rule 5 intends. Plain
		# emitting = true may only preprocess the first time (brief, Unconfirmed Q3). No embers are
		# erased: a K.O., the result screen and the 1 s intro always take longer than the 2.5 s
		# lifetime. (Claude Code, under Zhaohui's delegation, 2026-11-08.)
		embers.restart()
	elif _in_fight and not fight:
		embers.emitting = false      # rule 1: stop emitting; live particles finish their lifetime
	_in_fight = fight
	_apply_speed()

beats.narration_text: Here's the K.O. Emission stops, and the last embers fade out. Then the rematch, and the field is back at once.

beats.narration_text: Three ways to stop time, and they're different. The game's pause and hitstop: speed scale zero, frozen on every tick. Pausing the scene tree: the node stops by itself. Hidden: the brief said particles keep ageing, but the test found they freeze, and never finish while hidden. Jow-hway chose option one: revise the rule to what Godot actually does. The evidence is indirect: node flags over time.

show.event: three states and the hidden finding; Pause card lights

props.title: Three Ways To Stop Time
props.source: Source: TEST-REPORT.md A6 (state tests, open finding); CHANGE-BRIEF.md Revision 4; logs/test_embers_state_60fps.log

beats.narration_text: Now the process step as a GPU shader. Jow-hway converted the hit spark to a GPU node in the editor and saved the shader Godot generated. Line one thirty-seven mixes the minimum and maximum speed per particle: the brief's fifteen to seventy-five. Line two sixty sends it in a random direction inside the spread. Lines three oh seven and three twenty turn gravity into velocity. And a finding: the conversion dropped the colour ramp and the scale curve. Every particle gets one constant colour.

show.event: four lines beside four brief settings; Line 137 card lights

beats.narration_text: What did the tests prove? The config tests read every setting back from the scene files: sixty-nine and eighty-five checks, none failed. The state tests drive the real loop with real input: a burst for each of sixteen hits, none for thirty-one blocks and whiffs, frozen in pause and hitstop. Then Jow-hway broke the scene twice. A Godot three property name loads with no error at all, and the sparks just got slower. Only the read-back caught it, and a drifted amount too.

show.event: suites and mutations; Config card lights

props.title: What The Tests Proved
props.source: Source: TEST-REPORT.md A6; logs/test_hit_spark_*, test_embers_*, mutation_a6_1_*, mutation_a6_2_*

beats.narration_text: And the price. Measured headless on the CPU, medians: the spark costs about a hundredth of a millisecond per frame, the embers six thousandths, against budgets of a quarter and a half. A GPU particle effect would read near zero headless, because its process is a shader and the dummy renderer runs none. These are CPU nodes, but the GPU still draws them, so GPU time counts too. The Visual Profiler read zero here, so Claude Code measured GPU render time in a window instead: plus twelve and plus four thousandths. Far under budget.

show.event: the price table and the two notes; CPU card lights

props.title: Both Prices, Under Budget
props.status: MEASURED · cost_effects.gd (headless CPU) · gpu_price.gd (windowed GPU, Claude Code)
props.source: Source: TEST-REPORT.md A6 (Headless CPU price, GPU price); CHANGE-BRIEF.md short answer 4; logs/cost_effects_60fps.log, gpu_price_windowed.log

beats.narration_text: What no headless run can show is what a particle looks like: whether it reads on the lantern glow, or whether the embers are too faint. That's the strips and Jow-hway's eyes. Jow-hway's whole in-play report: when I ran the game, everything was normal, no problems. Recorded as given; it doesn't name rapid repeats or the lantern one by one. And the pool's all-four-busy fallback was never reached in a test.

props.title: What No Headless Run Shows
props.source: Source: TEST-REPORT.md A6 (In play, HUMAN CHECK); README.md A6 known limitations

beats.narration_text: The agents made mistakes, and the checks caught them. The first cost script measured itself, until an empty-scene control showed every case reading the same. An agent ran the texture generator through the test wrapper, then deleted that log. Its star-shape check failed its own texture. The pool trusted a late finished signal after a round reset. And several commands were denied. And Claude read one strip wrong: it predicted the spark's edge would stay put.

show.event: seven caught mistakes; Cost card lights

props.title: Mistakes The Checks Caught
props.status: RECORD · FRICTIONAL.md A6, TEST-REPORT.md A6, TUNING.md
props.source: Source: FRICTIONAL.md A6 (steps 2, 3/5, 7, tuning); TEST-REPORT.md A6; TUNING.md Effect A r1

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: every setting read back, one spark per hit, embers only during the fight, both frozen in pause, two mutations that fail, and both prices far under budget. Uncertain: hidden embers freeze only by indirect evidence, the round reset needs test setup, the GPU price isn't from the profiler, and the spark still has no impact direction. Jow-hway wrote the brief, the predictions and the verdicts, ran every capture and made the mutations. Claude Code built the scenes, controllers and tests and read the strips, and approved the later agent steps after Jow-hway said: do the rest yourself. Both textures are drawn by code. Next step: give the spark a direction.
